FIRST read /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/AGENT-BRIEF.md in full and obey it. You own billing/Stripe code (lib/stripe.ts, worker/billing.ts, card-save flows, renewal / admin 'Renew now'); no other agent edits it. IMPORTANT SCOPE LIMIT: do NOT use any live-mode Stripe key or call the live Stripe API at all (not even read-only). Work from the database, code, logs and Stripe TEST mode only (test keys, if present in /opt/nxeon-staging/.env or the test config; if none exist, build with mocked Stripe responses and say so).

PROBLEM (live, revenue-impacting): renewals charging a saved card fail with Stripe: 'The provided PaymentMethod was previously used with a PaymentIntent without Customer attachment, shared with a connected account without Customer attachment, or was detached from a Customer. It may not be used again. To use a PaymentMethod multiple times, you must attach it to a Customer first.' Seen 14 times in the last 7 days of worker logs (`journalctl -u nxeon-worker --since '7 days ago' | grep 'previously used with a PaymentIntent'`), e.g. customer 'bujangsmp' (server bujangsmp, owner ustazwanamirul@gmail.com, Minecraft 4GB, expired 2026-09-30, auto-renew ON, locked renewal price $8.99; admin 'Renew now' shows '$2.79 wallet + $6.20 card' then this error). The PaymentCard table has 49 rows (id,userId,stripePaymentMethodId,brand,last4,expMonth,expYear,isPrimary,createdAt — no Stripe customer reference). Earlier history: only one card renewal had ever succeeded in prod before the admin Renew-now work.
INVESTIGATE: (1) every code path that creates/saves a PaymentMethod (Checkout sessions, wallet top-ups, add-card flows; lib/stripe.ts around lines 154/228/323) and which omit `customer` / `setup_future_usage:'off_session'` / a SetupIntent so the PM is consumed as a one-off guest PM; whether User has a stable Stripe customer id and where it is stored; (2) from the DB and logs only, estimate which saved cards are likely unusable (cards saved via the broken path vs the fixed path, by createdAt/flow) and which customers have failed charges recently (worker/billing.ts logs + Invoice/WalletTransaction/EmailLog); (3) what the renewal worker does on failure today — retries ('transient charge error'), grace period, when it suspends, what customers are emailed, whether paying customers get suspended because of OUR bug — and quantify who is at risk in the next 7 days (servers expiring + auto-renew + card path + insufficient wallet) using DB queries.
FIX: correct card capture so every saved card is attached to a Customer and usable off-session (Checkout `customer` + `payment_intent_data.setup_future_usage`, or SetupIntent), lazily create/store the Customer, migrate existing users safely; make renewals robust: Customer-attached PM + off-session confirm, handle SCA/authentication_required (email a confirm-payment link), classify errors (permanent card errors vs transient) and stop retrying a permanent PM failure as if transient, a sane dunning ladder (notify day 0/1/3 with a working 'update card' link, a grace period before suspension — never suspend or destroy because of a platform-side card problem; warnings first), wallet-first-then-card logic preserved; in the customer portal a clear 're-add your card' banner for unusable saved cards (Nexion style, minimal edit); in admin a list/count of at-risk customers with a one-click 'send re-add-card email' (write the email template; do NOT send real emails in dev) and a per-server grace-extension action. Integer cents, idempotency keys per invoice/period, no double charges, audit-logged.
TEST: Stripe TEST mode end-to-end if test keys exist: a card saved via the new flow is attached and a later off-session renewal succeeds; the old flow reproduces the exact error; SCA-required test card path; dunning state-machine unit tests. NEVER create charges, customers or PMs in live mode; never touch real customers' cards. Provide the owner an exact step list: deploy, then a dry-run-first script to flag/notify affected customers, plus a safe manual remedy for bujangsmp today (e.g. Extend by N days via the admin action — don't execute it).

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

new_string.description: The text to replace it with (must be different from old_string)

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences of old_string (default false)

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

24	 * key, so the browser mounts Stripe Embedded Checkout in a modal on OUR page
25	 * (components/customer/StripeCheckoutModal) — nobody is redirected to Stripe.

38	 * constructor, so webhooks, retrieves and every other money call keep the SDK's

75	 * is no longer JSON, and the consumer's `JSON.parse` throws inside a `try` that
76	 * returns `null` on failure — at which point `fulfilCheckoutSession` cannot see an
77	 * order, a resize or a disk expansion in the session, and falls through to its
78	 * plain wallet-top-up branch. The customer's card is charged, the money lands in

84	 * at confirm time — nothing has been charged at this point." That reasoning

87	 * have paid nothing, which is the cheapest possible moment to fail.

110	 * card form AND the 3D Secure challenge inside an iframe on our own page.

112	 * feel), but it's measurably less robust than a full-page redirect for a

118	 * seconds after being asked to authenticate — too fast for a real completed
119	 * bank challenge, consistent with the iframe never successfully loading.

128	 * SAME metadata (so the existing `fulfilCheckoutSession` dispatch handles it

132	 * open (already paid, or expired) — nothing to retry.

135	  originalSessionId: string,
136	): Promise<{ url: string } | null> {
137	  if (!stripeConfigured()) return null;
138	  const original = await stripe().checkout.sessions.retrieve(originalSessionId, {
139	    expand: ["line_items"],
140	  });
141	  if (original.status !== "open") return null;
142	  const base = process.env.APP_URL ?? "http://localhost:3000";
143	  const lineItems = (original.line_items?.data ?? []).map((li) => ({
144	    price_data: {
145	      currency: original.currency ?? "usd",
146	      product_data: { name: li.description || "Nxeon order" },
147	      unit_amount: li.price?.unit_amount ?? li.amount_total,
148	    },
149	    quantity: li.quantity ?? 1,
150	  }));
151	  if (lineItems.length === 0) return null;
152	  const session = await stripe().checkout.sessions.create({
153	    mode: "payment",
154	    customer: typeof original.customer === "string" ? original.customer : undefined,
155	    payment_intent_data: { setup_future_usage: "off_session" },
156	    expires_at: Math.floor((Date.now() + ORDER_CHECKOUT_EXPIRES_MS) / 1000),
157	    line_items: lineItems,

159	    // generic across every order type: fulfilment reads metadata, not ui_mode.
160	    metadata: original.metadata ?? undefined,

235	    expires_at: Math.floor((Date.now() + ORDER_CHECKOUT_EXPIRES_MS) / 1000),
236	    line_items: [

241	          unit_amount: amountCents,
242	        },
243	        quantity: 1,

245	    ],

247	      nxeonUserId: user.id,

268	    return_url: `${base}/api/stripe/confirm?session_id={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID}`,

Customers already seem attached during order checkouts, so I'm digging deeper into stripe.ts, stripe-cards.ts, and the charging logic in worker/billing.ts to find the gap. I want to check if any checkout sessions, like wallet top-ups, skip attaching a customer, and trace how a card actually gets saved into PaymentCard from the payment intent during checkout session crediting.

If a payment method was saved from a PI without a customer—possibly from older code before ensureStripeCustomer existed—that PM could be unusable now even though the PaymentCard row still persists. I want to verify whether setup_future_usage combined with a customer on the session reliably attaches the PM, or if there's a historical mismatch I need to trace across these files.

1	import { vpsTerm, vpsTermPriceCents, termPriceCents } from "./billing-terms";
2	import { extraDiskCentsAt } from "./extra-disk";
3	import { type BackupTier, backupTierMonthlyCents } from "./backup-tiers";
4	import { partnerDiscountCentsFor } from "./partner-discount";
5	
6	/**
7	 * What one renewal costs — the SINGLE definition, used by every path that quotes
8	 * or charges one: the automatic sweep in worker/billing.ts, the saved-card path,
9	 * the "Renew now" button, the server page and the deploy wizard's term cards.
10	 *
11	 * WHY IT LIVES IN ITS OWN FILE. It used to sit in lib/stripe-cards.ts, which
12	 * imports the Stripe SDK and (transitively) nodemailer. The moment a CLIENT
13	 * component — the deploy wizard — needed the renewal price, that import chain
14	 * dragged `nodemailer/lib/dkim` into the browser bundle and the build failed with
15	 * "Can't resolve 'fs'". The pricing rule is pure arithmetic and has no business
16	 * carrying a mail transport with it, so it lives here with only the two tiny
17	 * modules it genuinely needs. lib/stripe-cards.ts re-exports it, so no server-side
18	 * caller had to change.
19	 *
20	 * The rule this file exists to enforce: there is ONE renewal formula. Two
21	 * incidents in one day came from a second copy — first a button that hardcoded
22	 * "+30 days" and the monthly price while the action charged a full term ($8.99
23	 * shown, $97.09 taken), then the shared quote written to fix it, which computed
24	 * from `plan.priceCents` and so ignored `gamePlan` and would have billed a $4.99
25	 * game server at its $8.99 base plan. Do not add a second formula.
26	 */
27	export type RenewalCharge = {
28	  months: number;
29	  /**
30	   * The amount to CHARGE / display — tax-INCLUSIVE (net + tax). When no
31	   * `taxRatePercent` is supplied (the default), tax is 0 and this equals `netCents`,
32	   * so every existing caller is unchanged. Because display and charge both read this
33	   * one field, `displayed === charged === renewed` holds by construction.
34	   */
35	  totalCents: number;
36	  /** The pre-tax subtotal (plan + IP + disk + backup). Invoice line items sum to this. */
37	  netCents: number;
38	  /** The VAT/GST added on top of `netCents` (Finding 1); 0 when no rate was passed. */
39	  taxCents: number;
40	  /** The rate (%) `taxCents` was computed at, recorded on the invoice. */
41	  taxRatePercent: number;
42	  /** The extra-root-disk portion, which gets its own invoice line. */
43	  extraDiskCents: number;
44	  extraDiskMonthlyCents: number;
45	  /** The paid backup-tier portion (Plus retention), which gets its own invoice line. */
46	  backupCents: number;
47	  backupMonthlyCents: number;
48	  /**
49	   * The dedicated-IP surcharge portion of `netCents` (0 unless
50	   * `dedicatedIpBillable`) — broken out as its OWN field (added 2026-09-26, purely
51	   * additive) so a caller can record it on `Invoice.dedicatedIpCents` for the
52	   * Creator Partner Program's commission rule (a dedicated IP add-on earns a
53	   * partner 0% commission — see lib/partner-commission.ts commissionableBaseCents).
54	   * Previously this amount was only ever folded into the combined subtotal with no
55	   * way to recover it after the fact.
56	   */
57	  ipCents: number;
58	  /**
59	   * How much of `netCents` was shaved off by a one-time RETENTION OFFER
60	   * (`PricedServer.pendingRenewalDiscountPercent`) on THIS renewal. 0 for every
61	   * server that never went through the cancel-flow retention offer (the
62	   * overwhelming majority) — existing callers that never read this field see no
63	   * behavior change. Exists so the invoice can show the discount as its own
64	   * line, the same way `extraDiskCents`/`backupCents` get their own lines,
65	   * instead of silently folding it into a smaller plan line.
66	   */
67	  retentionDiscountCents: number;
68	  /**
69	   * How much of `netCents` was shaved off by the CREATOR PARTNER PROGRAM's
70	   * permanent recurring discount (10% off every renewal, forever, once attached —
71	   * see lib/partner-discount.ts). 0 for every server owned by a customer not
72	   * attached to an active partner (the overwhelming majority) — existing callers
73	   * that never pass `RenewalPrices.partnerDiscountPercent` see zero behavior
74	   * change. Applied AFTER the one-time retention offer (if any), on whatever is
75	   * left, so the two discounts stack rather than double-count the same dollar.
76	   */
77	  partnerDiscountCents: number;
78	  /** The recurring rate `partnerDiscountCents` was computed at (0 when not attached). */
79	  partnerDiscountPercent: number;
80	  /** Human label for the invoice / receipt ("Nebula VPS" or the game plan name). */
81	  label: string;
82	};
83	
84	export type PricedServer = {
85	  termMonths: number;
86	  extraDiskGB: number;
87	  plan: { name: string; priceCents: number };
88	  gamePlan: { name: string; priceCents: number; termMonths: number } | null;
89	  dedicatedIp: unknown | null;
90	  /**
91	   * Did the customer actually choose/pay for this IP, vs. a VPS just being
92	   * handed one for free by the `dedicated_ip_default` platform setting? See the
93	   * IP surcharge lines below for why this has to gate the charge alongside
94	   * `dedicatedIp` itself.
95	   */
96	  wantsDedicatedIp: boolean;
97	  /** Paid backup retention tier. A full Server row supplies it; synthetic callers must pass it. */
98	  backupTier: BackupTier;
99	  /**
100	   * The ANNUAL discount FROZEN on this server at sale (`Server.annualDiscountPct`),
101	   * or null on a legacy/monthly/flat row. OPTIONAL so the many synthetic
102	   * `PricedServer` display/quote objects keep compiling; a full Server row supplies
103	   * it automatically. When present it WINS over the live `prices.annualDiscountPct`,
104	   * so an annual VPS / NxCloud / game server renews at exactly the rate it was
105	   * SOLD at even if the admin retunes the setting afterwards; null falls back to
106	   * the live rate, which for every non-annual term is identical maths.
107	   */
108	  annualDiscountPct?: number | null;
109	  /**
110	   * GRANDFATHER PROGRAM (2026-09-17): the plan/game-plan monthly rate FROZEN
111	   * on this server at sale (`Server.grandfatheredRenewalCents`), read here
112	   * INSTEAD OF the live `plan.priceCents` / `gamePlan.priceCents` when
113	   * present. OPTIONAL, same shape as `annualDiscountPct` above — every
114	   * existing synthetic `PricedServer` (wizard previews, tests) keeps
115	   * compiling and keeps pricing off the live catalog rate exactly as
116	   * before; only a real Server row (which supplies it automatically)
117	   * actually grandfathers anything. Null/undefined = price off the live
118	   * plan, which is correct for a legacy pre-program row that was never
119	   * backfilled AND for a free/admin server with no real price to freeze.
120	   */
121	  grandfatheredRenewalCents?: number | null;
122	  /**
123	   * RETENTION OFFER (2026-09-17 field, wired 2026-09-19): the one-time percent
124	   * FROZEN on this server's `pendingRenewalDiscountPercent` when a customer
125	   * accepted the "stay and save" cancel-flow offer (lib/actions-server-lifecycle.ts
126	   * claimRetentionOffer). Unlike `grandfatheredRenewalCents` (a permanent
127	   * per-month price override), this discounts exactly ONE upcoming renewal
128	   * charge and the caller is responsible for clearing it back to null once that
129	   * renewal actually commits (see worker/billing.ts commitRenewal and
130	   * lib/actions.ts renewNow) — `renewalCharge` itself only reads it, it never
131	   * decides when the discount has been "used up". OPTIONAL / null = no pending
132	   * discount, which is every server that has never gone through the retention
133	   * flow (and is therefore identical to today's behavior).
134	   */
135	  pendingRenewalDiscountPercent?: number | null;
136	};
137	
138	/**
139	 * The admin-priced inputs a renewal is charged against. Every field is REQUIRED
140	 * deliberately, mirroring how the codebase guards renewal pricing everywhere else
141	 * (`termPromoPercent` is likewise required in lib/proration.ts): a call site that
142	 * builds this object cannot silently forget one and fall back to a stale default.
143	 */
144	export type RenewalPrices = {
145	  ipMonthlyCents: number;
146	  extraDiskPerGbCents: number;
147	  backupPlusCents: number;
148	  /**
149	   * The admin-configured ANNUAL discount (percent), resolved from the
150	   * `annual_discount_percent` setting via `annualDiscountPct()`.
151	   *
152	   * REQUIRED — not optional. A 12-month server renews at
153	   * `vpsTermPriceCents(price, 12, annualDiscountPct)`; if a call site could OMIT
154	   * this it would silently price annual at the shipped default (10%) while the
155	   * owner had set, say, 20% — the rate the customer was shown and charged at order.
156	   * Required turns that into a compile error at every one of the ~8 places that
157	   * build this object, so the annual setting cannot be forgotten on any renewal
158	   * path and `displayed === charged === renewed` holds.
159	   */
160	  annualDiscountPct: number;
161	  /**
162	   * OPTIONAL destination VAT/GST rate (percent) for the customer who owns this
163	   * server, resolved from their billing country (lib/tax.ts taxContextForUser).
164	   * Omitted / 0 => no tax added and `totalCents === netCents`, so every call site
165	   * that does not opt in is byte-for-byte unchanged. A charge site passes the
166	   * OWNER's rate so the wallet debit, the card leg and the invoice all agree; a
167	   * display of the owner's own renewal passes the SAME rate so the figure shown
168	   * equals the figure taken.
169	   */
170	  taxRatePercent?: number;
171	  /**
172	   * CREATOR PARTNER PROGRAM (2026-09-26): the customer's permanent RECURRING
173	   * discount percent (10 if attached to an active partner, 0 otherwise — resolved
174	   * by lib/partner-pricing.ts's `partnerDiscountForRenewal`, which always
175	   * collapses to the recurring tier since a renewal is never anyone's first
176	   * purchase). OPTIONAL, defaulting to 0 — every existing caller that doesn't
177	   * resolve/pass it keeps renewing at exactly today's price, byte-for-byte.
178	   */
179	  partnerDiscountPercent?: number;
180	};
181	
182	export function renewalCharge(
183	  server: PricedServer,
184	  prices: RenewalPrices,
185	): RenewalCharge {
186	  const isGame = !!server.gamePlan;
187	  // The term to renew — the customer's chosen `Server.termMonths` (1 = monthly,
188	  // 12 = annual). A game term is now a per-order choice (Monthly / Annual) just like
189	  // a VPS, so it rides the Server row, not the plan.
190	  //
191	  // VPS/NxCloud terms are always one of the 4 standard `VPS_TERMS`, so we normalise
192	  // through `vpsTerm`. A GAME server, however, may historically carry ANY term the
193	  // plan was configured with (a pre-existing game server was created with
194	  // `termMonths = gamePlan.termMonths`, which the admin can set 1..36). We therefore
195	  // read the game term back RAW (clamped >= 1) rather than through `vpsTerm`, whose
196	  // fallback would collapse a non-standard legacy value (say 3) to monthly and
197	  // change that server's renewal cadence. For the seeded games (all `termMonths: 1`)
198	  // and any new Monthly/Annual order this is identical to the standard path.
199	  const months = isGame ? Math.max(1, Math.round(server.termMonths)) : vpsTerm(server.termMonths).months;
200	  // The annual discount to price the term at: the rate FROZEN on the server at sale,
201	  // falling back to the live setting for legacy/monthly rows. Both halves resolve
202	  // the same number, so an annual sub renews at the sold rate.
203	  const annualPct = server.annualDiscountPct ?? prices.annualDiscountPct;
204	  // Extra root disk is billed EVERY cycle at the current per-GB price. Game plans
205	  // are a flat all-in price and never carry the add-on lines.
206	  const extraDiskMonthlyCents = isGame ? 0 : extraDiskCentsAt(server.extraDiskGB, prices.extraDiskPerGbCents);
207	  const extraDiskCents = extraDiskMonthlyCents * months;
208	  // Paid backup retention (Plus) rides alongside extra disk: billed every cycle at
209	  // the current admin price, and — like every add-on line — NOT carried by a game
210	  // plan (renewalCharge's game branch is flat all-in, so game servers are never
211	  // sold a paid backup tier; see lib/backup-upgrade.ts's game guard).
212	  const backupMonthlyCents = isGame ? 0 : backupTierMonthlyCents(server.backupTier, prices.backupPlusCents);
213	  const backupCents = backupMonthlyCents * months;
214	  // GRANDFATHER PROGRAM: the frozen rate wins over the live catalog price when
215	  // set (see PricedServer.grandfatheredRenewalCents's own doc comment) — this
216	  // is the ONE substitution point for both branches below, so a price rise on
217	  // the live Plan/GamePlan row never touches a server that already has a
218	  // frozen rate, while every other renewal-formula behavior (term math, annual
219	  // discount, add-ons) is completely unchanged.
220	  const grandfatheredPriceCents = server.grandfatheredRenewalCents ?? null;
221	  // A game plan's `priceCents` is its MONTHLY base (every seed is `termMonths: 1`).
222	  // Divide by the plan's own term so an admin plan configured as, say, a 3-month
223	  // bundle still yields a per-month rate; then price the customer's chosen term
224	  // through the SAME formula VPS uses. For a monthly game server this is exactly
225	  // `priceCents`; an ANNUAL game server renews at 12× that, less the annual discount.
226	  const gameMonthlyCents = isGame
227	    ? Math.round((grandfatheredPriceCents ?? server.gamePlan!.priceCents) / Math.max(1, server.gamePlan!.termMonths))
228	    : 0;
229	  // LEGACY GUARD. Game servers sold BEFORE terms existed carry no frozen annual rate
230	  // (`annualDiscountPct == null`) and always renewed at the plan's FLAT `priceCents`,
231	  // with no term discount ever applied. Preserve that exactly so no pre-existing game
232	  // server's renewal moves — only servers sold through the new term-aware flow (which
233	  // always stamps a frozen `annualDiscountPct`) are priced with `termPriceCents`.
234	  //
235	  // GUARD ON isGame FIRST. This value is only USED in the isGame branch below, but a
236	  // bare ternary evaluates it for EVERY server — and a VPS `PricedServer` (e.g. the one
237	  // the deploy wizard builds, `gamePlan: null`, no `annualDiscountPct`) then hits the
238	  // `annualDiscountPct == null` arm and dereferences `server.gamePlan!.priceCents` on a
239	  // null, crashing the whole deploy page with "Cannot read properties of null". Compute
240	  // 0 for non-game so the null is never touched.
241	  const gameTotalCents = !isGame
242	    ? 0
243	    : server.annualDiscountPct == null
244	      ? (grandfatheredPriceCents ?? server.gamePlan!.priceCents)
245	      : termPriceCents(gameMonthlyCents, months, annualPct);
246	  // Bill the IP surcharge only when the server BOTH actually holds a dedicated
247	  // IP AND the customer chose/paid for it (`wantsDedicatedIp`). Requiring
248	  // `dedicatedIp` alone used to mean two very different bugs at different times:
249	  // a NAT-fallback server (paid for an IP, pool was empty, never got one) being
250	  // charged for an IP it never received, and — found 2026-09-15 via a real
251	  // customer's admin profile showing a $2.99 "committed MRR" they never agreed
252	  // to — the opposite case: a VPS granted a dedicated IP for FREE by the
253	  // `dedicated_ip_default` platform setting (see worker/index.ts's provision())
254	  // being silently billed for it anyway on the next renewal. Requiring BOTH
255	  // flags fixes both directions: no charge without the address, no charge
256	  // without genuine customer intent to pay for it.
257	  const dedicatedIpBillable = !!server.dedicatedIp && server.wantsDedicatedIp;
258	  const ipCents = dedicatedIpBillable ? prices.ipMonthlyCents * months : 0;
259	  const preRetentionNetCents = isGame
260	    ? gameTotalCents + ipCents
261	    : vpsTermPriceCents(grandfatheredPriceCents ?? server.plan.priceCents, months, annualPct) +
262	      ipCents +
263	      extraDiskCents +
264	      backupCents;
265	  // RETENTION OFFER: a one-time percent-off THIS renewal only (see
266	  // PricedServer.pendingRenewalDiscountPercent's own doc comment). Applied to
267	  // the WHOLE pre-tax subtotal — plan plus every add-on line — because "50% off
268	  // your next renewal" is a single-event promise about the bill, not about one
269	  // line on it. Clamped 0..100 so a corrupt/out-of-range stored value can never
270	  // produce a negative charge or mint a discount beyond what was ever written
271	  // (claimRetentionOffer only ever writes 50). Applied BEFORE tax, matching
272	  // every other discount on this platform (coupons, promos) — the customer is
273	  // taxed on what they actually pay, not on the list price.
274	  const pendingDiscountPercent = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, server.pendingRenewalDiscountPercent ?? 0));
275	  const retentionDiscountCents =
276	    pendingDiscountPercent > 0 ? Math.round((preRetentionNetCents * pendingDiscountPercent) / 100) : 0;
277	  const afterRetentionCents = preRetentionNetCents - retentionDiscountCents;
278	  // CREATOR PARTNER PROGRAM: the customer's permanent 10%-off-every-renewal rate
279	  // (0 for the overwhelming majority never attached to a partner), applied to
280	  // whatever is left AFTER the one-time retention offer — the two stack rather
281	  // than either double-counting the same dollar or one silently cancelling the
282	  // other. Same clamp discipline as the retention percent above.
283	  const partnerDiscountPercent = Math.max(0, Math.min(100, prices.partnerDiscountPercent ?? 0));
284	  const partnerDiscountCents = partnerDiscountCentsFor(afterRetentionCents, partnerDiscountPercent);
285	  const netCents = afterRetentionCents - partnerDiscountCents;
286	  // VAT/GST on the pre-tax subtotal. Default rate 0 keeps `totalCents === netCents`
287	  // for every caller that does not pass the owner's rate (Finding 1).
288	  const taxRatePercent =
289	    Number.isFinite(prices.taxRatePercent) && (prices.taxRatePercent ?? 0) > 0 ? prices.taxRatePercent! : 0;
290	  const taxCents = Math.round((netCents * taxRatePercent) / 100);
291	  return {
292	    months,
293	    netCents,
294	    taxCents,
295	    taxRatePercent,
296	    totalCents: netCents + taxCents,
297	    extraDiskCents,
298	    extraDiskMonthlyCents,
299	    ipCents,
300	    partnerDiscountCents,
301	    partnerDiscountPercent,
302	    backupCents,
303	    backupMonthlyCents,
304	    retentionDiscountCents,
305	    label: isGame ? server.gamePlan!.name : `${server.plan.name} VPS`,
306	  };
307	}

I'm noticing that the PaymentCard rows all share identical creation timestamps and sequential IDs, which suggests these were backfilled rather than created organically — and I'm comparing payment method ID prefixes to see how they increment over time to spot which records look synthetic versus genuine.

The pm_1UA9w card appears to have been created at Stripe around early September but only written into the PaymentCard table on 09-24 — a backfill. This lines up with the incident where customers had successful charges but no saved card, implying someone backfilled rows from PaymentIntents' payment_method field, likely from PIs without an attached customer, making the PM unusable — exactly matching the error. I want to verify this by checking git history for a backfill script around that date and looking at AuditLog entries, and also figure out where the original 09-14 batch's payment method IDs came from before migration into this table.

My hypothesis is that these 9 cards came from Checkout sessions lacking a customer field, which would prevent Stripe from attaching the payment method even with setup_future_usage set. I'm trying to figure out which code path could produce a session without a customer when current code since 08-20 always includes one — possibly a hosted checkout fallback path, though I can't immediately see how Link or wallet payments would bypass attachment either.

I need to pull up the backfill script and audit logs, check servers at risk in the next 7 days, look into the bujangsmp server's dunning state and email history, and review billing.ts around renewal/commitment logic and the suspension/sweep/autoRecharge sections. I should also skim lib/stripe.ts's createCustomCheckout section for how payment methods get saved, and gather the list of payment-failure emails that need to be written.

I also need to locate the admin "Renew now" UI and action, the customer billing page banner, and figure out the test directory structure and how tests are run via package.json scripts.

I'm checking whether the backfill's comparison logic would have skipped detached payment methods since they have a null customer field, then tracing ustazwanamirul's case where a card removal event on 08-30 would have cleared the user's stripePaymentMethodId through the detach/clear flow.

So the real mystery is how that field got re-populated afterward with the removed Visa card. Adopting unclaimed cards wouldn't pick up a detached PM since it's no longer attached at Stripe, which points instead to a possible manual, uncommitted backfill script run around the time of the 09-24 fix — one that pulled the payment method straight from each customer's latest PaymentIntent rather than checking attachment status, which would explain writing back a PM that was already detached.

Looking at the pm_ id itself, its timestamp suggests it was created around Sep 8-9, after the Aug 30 removal — meaning the customer paid again after removing the card, and whatever checkout flow handled that payment didn't attach the resulting PM to the customer. That narrows it to checkout paths missing `setup_future_usage` on the payment intent, like `createOutstandingCheckout` or `createOutstandingEmbedded`, which set a customer on the session but never request future reusability.

Checking fulfil-checkout, I find the generic top-up branch calls saveCardFromPaymentSession for any session with just nxeonUserId metadata, even outstanding-balance sessions that never set setup_future_usage. That's the actual bug: the dunning "settle balance" checkout ends up saving an unattached PM as the customer's primary card.

For ustaz, this means an unattached PM gets recorded as the primary card after paying an outstanding renewal via the settle link, so every later renewal fails. I'm uncertain how the backfill on 09-24 fits in, since it should have skipped unattached PMs by checking pm.customer against the stripeCustomerId — the cluster of PaymentCard rows written within seconds on that date suggests some script ran, possibly a modified version of the backfill, though I can't fully confirm the path it took.

Since I can't query live Stripe directly, I'll try to reproduce the failure in test mode instead — creating a raw payment method from a test token, confirming a PaymentIntent without a customer attached, then attempting to reuse that same payment method on a PaymentIntent that does have a customer, to see if it throws the expected error and capture its error code.

I should also check the actual database for evidence: wallet transactions and fulfilled sessions around the September 8 renewal date for this user. I notice the email log shows no payment-related emails were sent — only tickets and onboarding — which suggests the dunning flow treats this failure as transient and stays silent, quietly retrying every hour since September 30th. The suspend date would then be calculated as the minimum of the next dunning retry time or a capped window from expiry.

That means the server gets suspended on October 10th with zero emails sent, which needs fixing. Now I'm planning concrete work: in the stripe-cards library, I need to verify that payment methods belong to the correct customer before persisting them, and handle the case where a payment method isn't attached by attempting to attach it — if that fails, skip persistence and log an audit event instead of silently failing.

I should add setup_future_usage to the outstanding checkout sessions so cards get saved properly for dunning customers, since they most need a working card on file. I'm also tracing through what happens if Checkout creates a new customer via customer_creation defaults — the session's customer ID might differ from the user's stored stripeCustomerId, and since persistCard mirrors that customer onto the user record, I need to confirm this stays consistent since our flows always use ensureStripeCustomer first.

Now I'm thinking classifyChargeError needs to treat this specific invalid_request_error (the "previously used with a PaymentIntent without Customer attachment" message) as a permanent "unavailable" failure rather than transient, which would trigger forgetMissingPaymentMethod on the worker side. But I realize the underlying PaymentCard row would still exist and could get re-mirrored later via setPrimary, so I probably need a schema change to mark that card row as permanently unusable rather than just clearing the user's columns.

I'm now sketching the logic: mirrorPrimaryCardToUser should skip unusable cards, listPaymentCards should expose an unusable flag, the billing page should show a banner prompting the user to re-add their card, and the forget-logic should promote another usable card to primary if one exists. I'm also planning a verifyPaymentMethodAttached helper that checks if the payment method belongs to the customer and attempts to attach it if not, returning false on failure so persistCard can react accordingly. On the worker side, I'm thinking the unavailable branch in attemptCardRenewal should send a dedicated "card unusable" email with a re-add link instead of just a notification.

I'm reconsidering the suspension timing so that platform-caused card issues never trigger an immediate suspension -- warnings should come first. That means adding a grace period field on the server, where the suspension date becomes the later of the original date or this grace deadline, and layering in a dunning-style notification schedule (day 0, 1, 3) for the unusable-card case, though I'm trying to keep the implementation lean rather than adding a full notification-stage counter.

That chargeable-card grace period would silently suspend paying customers after 3 days — exactly the bug path I want to avoid. A cleaner fix is adding a `Server.billingGraceUntil` field that overrides the computed suspension date whenever it's later, setting it to at least 7 days out the first time an unusable card is detected, while still marking the card unusable and clearing its mirror state.

Since the card is gone, I still need a dunning-style reminder ladder in `renewDueServer` for this no-card case: a `nudgeCardReadd` call gated by `dunningNextAt` that fires immediately on detection, then again at +1 day and +3 days, each pointing to the update-card link, with a final warning a day before grace expires.

I also want admin tooling: an action to extend billing grace by a given number of days (audit-logged), and another to manually trigger the re-add-card email for a user. Then I'm thinking about an admin "at-risk customers" page, though that touches the admin shell A1 owns, so I'd just add a page under the existing billing admin route rather than restructure navigation.

I'm also sketching a migration/flagging script that checks each stored payment card against Stripe to confirm it's still attached to the right customer, flagging mismatches as unusable, with optional apply and notify flags.

For testing, I'll unit-test the classification logic with mocked payment method objects since I can't run this against real test cards, plus build out pure functions for card reusability checks and dunning grace period math, mirrored in the lib layer for testability, along with a staging-mode script that reproduces the original error and verifies the fix works end-to-end.

Then I need to update the customer portal's billing view to surface an "unusable card" state, and finally update the docs.

On the checkout side, I should also add `setup_future_usage: off_session` to the payment intent data for both regular and embedded checkout flows so future off-session charges work correctly, and tighten the save-card helper to only persist when actually attached. I also want to confirm the idempotency key scheme is safe for repeated hourly retries with the same failing card, and trace through what happens for the currently-affected customer once my fix lands: the card gets flagged unusable, the mirror is cleared, a 7-day grace period starts, and the customer gets notified -- while leaving the owner's manual extend-by-days remedy alone for now.

Next I want to gather several pieces in parallel: a sandboxed repro script using the staging test key (with a safety check to refuse live keys), the customer's wallet transactions and invoices around September to test my settle-link theory, the billing view component's card section, the top-up branch and session classification logic in the checkout fulfillment code, the admin area auth pattern and nav entries for billing pages, the mailer's build/template signatures and template registry, and finally the relevant documentation section on renewals and dunning so I know what to update.

5604:## Change history — the first 28 commits
## Renewals, card auto-charge and dunning

**What it does.** `worker/billing.ts` is the money engine. Every 10 minutes it warns about upcoming
renewals, charges everything that is due, retries failed cards on a fixed schedule, suspends what
never pays, and terminates what stays unpaid. It is the largest single behavioural surface in the
platform and the one where a mistake costs a customer their data.

**Trigger.** No cron and no systemd timer. It is an in-process interval inside the worker loop:
`/opt/nxeon/worker/index.ts:1153` (`if (Date.now() - lastSweep > 10 * 60_000)`) → `:1156`
`billingSweep()` → `:1162` `productRenewalSweep()`.

**Phase order** — `billingSweep()` at `/opt/nxeon/worker/billing.ts:232`:

```
 1  adoptUnclaimedCards(now)          :247   (before any card state is read)
 2  T-3d "renews soon" notification   :255   suppressed when the wallet covers it
                                             OR a chargeable card exists  :269
 3  dueServers(now)                   :293 → renewDueServer() per server  :303
 4  terminateOverdue(now, cfg)        :309
 5  cardExpirySweep                   :315
 6  autoRechargeSweep                 :320
 7  domainAutoRenewSweep              :325
 8  domainTransferInSweep             :330
```

`dueServers()` at `:211` selects `isFree: false`, `expiresAt: { lt: now }`,
`status: { in: ["RUNNING", "STOPPED"] }`. **Suspended servers are deliberately excluded** — which is
the root of the incident described in the next chapter.

**What a renewal costs — and there is exactly one definition of it.**
`renewalCharge(server, prices)` in `/opt/nxeon/lib/renewal-charge.ts:43` is the only place the number
is computed. `renewalQuote` (`/opt/nxeon/lib/renewal-quote.ts:45`) is a **presentation wrapper**: it
calls `renewalCharge` at `:49` and adds nothing but the duration phrasing the UI needs. It owns no
arithmetic at all, and `test/purchase-consent.test.ts:407-411` asserts the file contains none.

Given the disk constraints, I'll avoid running the dev server and instead rely on typecheck and node tests, skipping the database since the tests are pure. Checking the error reproduction, I confirm it has `code: undefined` with a `StripeInvalidRequestError` type, meaning classification needs to be based on the message content rather than the code.

Tracing through ustaz's case: a PaymentIntent with a customer but no setup_future_usage leaves the payment method unattached, producing the same error pattern as case B. Looking at the timeline, ustaz's card was removed on 08-30 at 15:30 (Visa ending 6300, expires 09/27), and I suspect that same card got re-added as a PaymentCard row on 09-24 — making this another instance of case D, the detached scenario.

Since the committed backfill script checks for a customer on the PM, a detached PM with no customer should've been skipped — so the 09-24 rows must've come from a different variant of the script, one that pulled payment methods directly off successful PaymentIntents instead. That would explain the "8 real paying customers with a successful charge and zero saved card" investigation: this variant wrote PaymentCard and User-mirror rows for those customers even when the card had been explicitly removed, which is both a technical bug and a consent issue — we'd be attempting to charge cards customers deliberately removed. I need to be direct about that in the report, then move on to checking the dataframe and start drafting the implementation plan.

Now I'm laying out the schema changes — adding nullable `unusableAt`/`unusableReason` fields to PaymentCard and a `billingGraceUntil` field to Server, all additive — and sketching the stripe-cards helper module with exported classification logic and a `persistCard` function that attaches the payment method before saving, refusing to persist if attachment fails.

I also need a `markPaymentMethodUnusable` function that flags a card unusable, demotes it from primary if needed and promotes the next usable card, and updates `mirrorPrimaryCardToUser` and `listPaymentCards` to respect the new unusable flag, while reworking the worker's `forgetMissingPaymentMethod` path to mark rows unusable with a "missing_at_stripe" reason instead of deleting them outright.

For checkout creation, I should ensure a Stripe customer exists even when one isn't set yet and pass `setup_future_usage: "off_session"` so future charges work off-session.

In the billing worker, when a charge is unavailable I want to mark the card unusable, start a grace period, email the user, and schedule a dunning ladder of reminders at increasing intervals before the grace period ends.

I'm simplifying the email templates to two: a card re-add required/reminder/final notice template, and planning to let `suspendDueAt` respect the grace period while adding admin tools to send re-add emails, extend grace periods, and surface card health in an admin dashboard page.

Then I'm sketching the billing view updates to show an "unusable card" banner and badge, plus a maintenance script to flag unusable cards via Stripe lookups with dry-run/apply/notify flags, and outlining a test file for Stripe card reuse scenarios.

I'm wondering whether that import actually connects to Prisma in tests, since the Prisma client instantiation is lazy and doesn't establish a connection until first used.

I'll separate the pure classification logic into a new standalone module with no db imports, and reuse it for the reusable-payment-method check too. I also want to write a TEST-mode verification script that exercises this classifier against real Stripe test-mode errors, runnable via tsx.

Since disk space is tight, I'll skip rendering the dev server and just typecheck, noting the UI wasn't visually verified. Before finishing, I should double-check remaining conventions by skimming the admin billing actions/page, the mailer build options, the AddCardButton component, and how the email template catalog registers entries for the admin previewer.

content.thinking:
It looks like dunningView isn't called anywhere outside the lib, so I'll still add an optional billingGraceUntil field to the mirror for consistency. Now I'm moving on to the mailer edit, worker edits, and the dunning-schedule mirror, starting with updating the worker's imports to replace the old missing-payment-method helper.

For the worker, I need to route the `unavailable` branch in attemptCardRenewal to a new handleUnusableCard function, make renewDueServer call nudgeCardReadd when grace is active and respect the grace period in suspendDueAt, clear billingGraceUntil during commitRenewal's CAS update, and pass through the failure reason in autoRechargeSweep's unavailable branch. I'm working out the nudgeCardReadd notification ladder using the existing dunningStage/dunningNextAt fields (unused in this no-card state), mapping stages 1 through 4 to the initial detection notice, day-1, day-3, and final reminders, and scheduling each stage's next check accordingly.

The dunningNextAt will always stay at or after expiresAt since the server is already due, so clearStaleDunning's period check won't wipe it out — confirmed fine. The dunningView used in the portal for no-card customers doesn't seem to have any callers, so I can skip handling it.

For the grace duration itself, I'm setting a 7-day platform-fault grace window from the moment of detection, with billingGraceUntil taking the max of any existing value and now+7d — this overrides the normal 3-day post-expiry suspension grace for no-card customers, pushing suspension out further.

I also want to check the T-3 day warning loop and renewal reminder sweep — both should still fire appropriately for card-less customers flagged by the script, giving them in-portal notices and pre-expiry emails, which seems acceptable. Now I'm extending suspendDueAt to factor in the new billingGraceUntil field when computing the suspension date.

I need to apply this same grace-period logic in both the worker and the shared lib, since the test tripwire only checks constants. I also need to make sure the worker's recordDeclinedAttempt passes billingGraceUntil through when calling suspendDueAt.

input.command:
cd /opt/nxeon-wt-billfix && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/DOCUMENTATION.md'
s=open(p).read()
trailer = "---\n\n*Companion docs: `CLAUDE.md`"
assert s.count(trailer)==1
section = r'''## Saved cards Stripe can never charge again — renewal failures, the fix, and the card-health tooling (2026-10-01)

**Symptom (live, revenue-impacting).** `journalctl -u nxeon-worker | grep 'previously used with a PaymentIntent'`
showed the same renewal (customer `bujangsmp`, Minecraft 4 GB, expired 2026-09-30, auto-renew on, wallet
$2.79 of the $8.99) failing EVERY HOUR with Stripe's *"The provided PaymentMethod was previously used with a
PaymentIntent without Customer attachment … or was detached from a Customer. It may not be used again."*
The admin **Renew now** button reported the same text as a "transient" error. No email ever went to the customer.

**Root cause — two halves.**

1. *The classification.* That Stripe error is `invalid_request_error` with **no `code`** (verified in TEST mode,
   `scripts/verify-card-reuse-testmode.ts`). `classifyChargeError` only knew `resource_missing`, so it fell to its
   safe default, **`transient`** → `attemptCardRenewal` rescheduled the SAME dead card an hour later, forever, in
   silence (transient never emails), while `suspendDueAt`'s slip cap meant the server would still have been
   SUSPENDED on day 10 (CARD_SUSPEND_DAY 6 + SUSPEND_SLIP_CAP_DAYS 4) with zero warnings. A paying customer, our bug.
2. *How dead cards got on file.* Stripe lets a PaymentMethod be reused ONLY while it is attached to a Customer.
   Verified in TEST mode: a PaymentIntent that carries `customer` but **not** `setup_future_usage` leaves the
   method **unattached** (`pm.customer = null`), and a detached method is dead for good — `paymentMethods.attach`
   is refused with the same wording. Two of our flows produced exactly that:
   - `createOutstandingCheckout` / `createOutstandingEmbedded` (the dunning "settle your balance" link and the
     in-portal "Pay now") set no `setup_future_usage` (and fell back to `customer_email` when no customer id was
     stored), yet their sessions fulfil as a plain **top-up**, and that branch of `fulfil-checkout.ts` calls
     `saveCardFromPaymentSession` — which recorded the unattached method as the customer's PRIMARY card.
   - The 2026-09-24 `PaymentCard` back-write (7 rows, ids `cmuf0qyzq…cmuf0r3c6`, written in one 4-second burst).
     **Six of those seven customers had explicitly REMOVED that exact card** weeks earlier (`card.removed` audit
     rows: ustazwanamirul 08-30, sandycoco 09-06, sasamihi 09-07, hero25455 09-07, loganwsmith 09-08, ssuplo 09-13),
     i.e. the methods were detached at Stripe. The committed `scripts/backfill-payment-cards.ts` checks
     `pm.customer === stripeCustomerId` and would have SKIPPED them, so a different (uncommitted) write produced
     these rows. Beyond the technical failure this is a consent problem: we were attempting to charge cards the
     customers had removed. `bujangsmp`'s "card" is the Visa ···· 6300 its owner removed on 2026-08-30.

**Who was exposed (prod DB, 2026-10-01).** 7 card-dependent renewals due within 7 days; 5 of them on the
09-24 rows: bujangsmp (expired 09-30), dst-ddvzfe (10-04), minecraft-i4qk6y (10-06), projectzomboid-kc0kcr (10-06,
wallet may cover), epicsauce69 (10-07). sausaugepro (09-14 row) and vps-v87z (organic 09-27 save) look healthy
but are "unvetted" until the flag script runs. 49 `PaymentCard` rows in total; the 20 written on 09-14 are the
documented table migration of cards saved through the attached path and should vet clean.

**The fix (branch `fix/stripe-saved-card-renewals`).**

- `lib/stripe-charge-errors.ts` (NEW, pure, no db/SDK): `classifyChargeError` now returns
  `{ kind: "unavailable", reason: "not_reusable" }` for the "may not be used again" wording (message-matched —
  there is no code), `reason: "missing_at_stripe"` for `resource_missing`; everything else unchanged (unknown → transient).
  `paymentMethodUnusableReason(pm, customerId)` is the single reusability rule (`pm.customer` must equal ours).
- `lib/stripe-cards.ts`: `persistCard` now **refuses** an unattached method (tries `attach` once for a fresh
  method, else writes `card.not_reusable` to AuditLog and records nothing) — every card-save path (setup session,
  payment session, adoption sweep) goes through it. `markPaymentMethodUnusable` retires a card: keeps the
  `PaymentCard` row, sets `unusableAt`/`unusableReason`, moves the primary flag to the next USABLE card, re-mirrors
  onto `User` (clearing `stripePaymentMethodId` when nothing usable is left). `mirrorPrimaryCardToUser` ignores
  retired rows; `setPrimaryPaymentCard` refuses them; `listPaymentCards` exposes `unusable`/`unusableReason`.
  Both outstanding-balance checkouts now ALWAYS resolve a Stripe Customer (`ensureStripeCustomer`) and set
  `payment_intent_data.setup_future_usage = "off_session"`, so a dunned customer who pays by card ends up with a
  card that works next month. `forgetMissingPaymentMethod(userId, reason)` routes through the retirement.
